lines: A worker is killed in the middle of a task.
The scheduler does exactly what it's supposed to do and retries it.
And by the time the data lands, twice as many rows come out as went in.
Nothing in the logs even says this happened.
Here's the trap. Retried does not mean it ran once, cleanly, and then ran again.
The first attempt may already have written its output, in full, before the scheduler ever lost track of it.
So a retry isn't a correctness mechanism on its own. It's only safe if running the exact same work twice does no harm.
Here's that idea measured directly, not just described.
The same three rows, written twice, two different ways.
One way writes to a file named for its own interval, and overwrites it each time. After two runs, it still holds three rows.
The other way appends instead. After the exact same two runs, it holds six.
Same task, same retry, same two runs. Only the write mode decided whether the retry was harmless or not.
Quick question first.
One task times out. A separate task hits a row that's simply malformed.
Does the executor retry both of those the same way?
Think it through before I answer.
steps.answer: No. A timeout is often transient and worth retrying. A malformed row is a data problem no retry fixes, so retrying it anyway just burns through attempts a real transient failure might have actually needed.

lines: Now a real three task workflow, run for real, not simulated.
The first task fails on purpose.
A second task, left on the default rule, never runs at all. Its real recorded state afterward is upstream failed.
A third task, told explicitly to run when something upstream fails, runs anyway, and succeeds.
Every one of those three states came straight out of a real metadata database after a real run.
Now the mechanism behind the scariest version of this: a worker that dies without telling anyone at all.
Airflow's own documented answer is a heartbeat. Every running task instance is expected to check in periodically.
When that heartbeat goes quiet for too long, the scheduler assumes the worker is gone, and marks the task failed, or retries it if it still can.
Notice the word assumes. The scheduler cannot actually know the task didn't just finish quietly a moment before it lost contact.
One more piece: a timeout caps how long any one task is allowed to run.
That's useful. But retrying something that was never going to succeed, over and over, doesn't make it more likely to succeed.
It just spends a limited budget of attempts on nothing, and delays the moment someone actually notices the real problem.
So: every task runs at least once, never exactly once.
An overwrite keyed to its own interval survives a retry untouched. An append does not.
Trigger rules decide who runs, who's skipped, and who becomes upstream failed, and we watched that happen for real.
And retries are a budget worth protecting, not a blanket fix for every kind of failure.
One more scenario.
Picture a task instance stuck on running for six hours straight. Nothing in its log complains. Nothing shows progress either.
What's actually worth checking first?
Take a second.
steps.answer: Its heartbeat. Nothing about looking like it's still running rules out a worker that already died silently — the heartbeat is the one honest signal, and it's exactly what the scheduler itself is watching.
